prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Pentago on a standard 6x6 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(you, opponent) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - The board is 6x6. - You are given two 6x6 arrays (or array-like objects) containing only 0/1 integers. - `you[r][c] == 1` means your marble is at row `r`, col `c`. - `opponent[r][c] == 1` means the opponent marble is at row `r`, col `c`. - An empty cell means `you[r][c] == 0` and `opponent[r][c] == 0`. - Positions are valid (no overlaps): never `you[r][c] == opponent[r][c] == 1`. - Quadrants are 3x3 sub-boards indexed as: - `quad = 0`: rows 1..3, cols 1..3 (top-left). - `quad = 1`: rows 1..3, cols 4..6 (top-right). - `quad = 2`: rows 4..6, cols 1..3 (bottom-left). - `quad = 3`: rows 4..6, cols 4..6 (bottom-right). - A quadrant rotation rotates the chosen 3x3 sub-board in place and affects BOTH players' marbles in that quadrant. - `L` is 90 degrees anticlockwise; `R` is 90 degrees clockwise. - After placement and rotation, a player wins if they have 5 (or more) marbles in a row in any straight line: horizontal, vertical, or diagonal (either diagonal direction). - If both players have a 5-in-a-row after your move is applied, the result is a draw. - If neither player has a 5-in-a-row and the board is full, the result is a draw. # Action / Return Format - Return a single string move formatted exactly as: `"row,col,quad,dir"`. - `row` is 1..6 (1-indexed). - `col` is 1..6 (1-indexed). - `quad` is 0..3. - `dir` is `L` or `R`. - A legal move must place exactly one of your marbles on an empty cell, then rotate exactly one quadrant 90 degrees in the chosen direction. - Example syntax: `"6,5,2,L"` means place at row 6 col 5, then rotate quadrant 2 left. - You may assume at least one empty cell exists (i.e., `policy` is not called when no legal move exists). # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm designing a Pentago policy using minimax with alpha-beta pruning and iterative deepening within a time budget, backed by bitboards for fast evaluation. With up to 288 possible moves per turn, I need to keep the search efficient and always fall back to any legal move if time runs out, using roughly 0.7s of the 1s budget.

I need to carefully check for wins created by both placement and rotation, since a quadrant rotation can inadvertently complete a line for either player, including simultaneous 5-in-a-rows resulting in a draw. For the board representation, I'm planning a 36-bit bitboard with fast quadrant extraction and precomputed rotation lookup tables so I can rotate any quadrant's 9 cells in one table lookup rather than iterating bit by bit, and I'll precompute all the winning lines of 5 across rows, columns, and diagonals for quick win detection.

Evaluating each move by counting my pieces versus the opponent's along each line for scoring works, but a naive depth-2 search checking every rotation combination is going to be too slow in Python given the raw operation count — I'll need to dedupe symmetric or redundant resulting positions (like rotating an empty quadrant) to cut down the branching factor.

I could also lean on alpha-beta pruning with strong move ordering to avoid fully expanding the opponent's reply nodes at depth 2, since a good first guess often lets me prune the rest early.

Now I'm sketching out the recursive minimax search function, checking for immediate wins and blocking necessary losses through terminal detection.

For move ordering, I'm considering sorting each node's children by their static evaluation before recursing, to make the alpha-beta pruning much more effective despite the extra evaluation cost.

I'm thinking through how to speed up the evaluation function itself, using bit_count for popcounts and iterating over the 32 line masks, scoring open lines for each side while skipping blocked ones — estimating this comes out to roughly 10 microseconds per evaluation call.

For time management, I'm planning to track elapsed time against a budget (around 0.7-0.8s of a 1-second limit) and only trust results from fully completed search depths, keeping root move ordering so the previously best move gets searched first at each new depth. I also want to make sure the search avoids handing the opponent a winning five-in-a-row unless we can match it, and rely on move deduplication to handle rotationally symmetric quadrants correctly.

For leaf-parent nodes, sorting is unnecessary since I need to evaluate every child anyway, so I'll just iterate and cut off early once a value drops below alpha; sorting only matters at deeper nodes where subtree cost justifies it. I'm estimating cost per root move at depth 2, weighing whether win-check overhead can be reduced since it's comparable to the eval cost itself.

I'm working out bitboard tricks to detect five-in-a-row efficiently, shifting and masking the 36-bit board for horizontal, vertical, and both diagonal directions with appropriate starting-position masks.

Writing bit-shift win detection...

Now I'm thinking about whether evaluation could be sped up similarly, considering precomputed lookup tables indexed by row bit patterns for my and opponent pieces to avoid the full 32-iteration line loop.

Vertical and diagonal lines make this harder since columns aren't stored contiguously. Estimating actual timing, I figure Python can handle maybe 20-30M simple ops/sec, so eval costs roughly 15µs, rotation another 3µs, win-check 3µs — around 22µs per child node, meaning the first move at depth 2 with 288 children takes about 6ms, with later moves benefiting from cutoffs.

Extending this out, most positions after cutoffs average maybe 30 children each, so the full depth-2 search should land around 0.2-0.3 seconds, with depth 3 mostly incomplete but partially explored. I'm also considering deduplication at the root and better move ordering using the exact values root children get from the previous iteration's depth-1 evaluation.

I'm also thinking about how the eval function should account for Pentago's rotation mechanic — a "4 in a row" threat isn't as decisive as in gomoku since rotations can neutralize it, but quadrant center cells stay rotation-invariant and are strategically valuable, so I want to give them a small positional bonus. I'm working out weighting for line counts, treating four-in-a-row with an open fifth cell as a real threat worth a meaningfully higher score than shorter lines.

Setting weight 4 to 50 with both-sided lines scoring zero, and I need to make sure array values get converted to ints properly. I'm now working out the rotation math, mapping each cell to its row/column, determining which quadrant it belongs to, and computing the local index within that quadrant for rotation.

Now I'm figuring out the bit extraction and insertion logic for each quadrant's 9-bit state, plus building lookup tables for clockwise and counterclockwise rotations by working out how row/column indices transform.

I'm considering combining extraction, rotation, and insertion into single precomputed tables per quadrant and direction to speed things up, then sketching how move generation would apply an empty cell placement followed by a quadrant rotation.

This gives just 8 rotation combos per node for cheap child generation, with each child computed as a simple OR of precomputed values. For terminal checks, I realize opponent's win-check depends only on the qd rotation, so I can precompute has5(op_rot) per qd — if that's already a win, any placement in that quadrant/rotation combo wins for the opponent.

I need to handle: if opponent gets 5 via this rotation, outcome is draw (0) if I also complete a 5, otherwise a loss. Also need a full-board draw check when all 36 cells are filled with no winner. For checking if my placement hits 5, I can skip the check cheaply if my piece count is under 5.

For the actual search, I'm defining a negamax function that returns the value for the side to move: terminal nodes get the win/draw/loss value, depth-1 nodes get a static evaluation from the mover's perspective, and deeper nodes recurse with negated bounds. At nodes with depth 2 or more, I want to order moves by their static evaluation to improve pruning, and I should dedupe children that produce the same resulting board pair.

I'll skip a transposition table for simplicity since the overhead isn't worth it here. For the static evaluation, I'm scoring each of the 32 lines by whether one side occupies it exclusively, weighting by piece count, plus a bonus for center control — I need to keep in mind this line-based heuristic won't catch every immediate four-in-a-row threat, but the depth-2 search should cover the most urgent tactical wins.

For time management, I'll check the clock before expanding each node using a high-resolution timer, throwing a timeout exception that the root catches to fall back on the last fully completed depth. The depth-1 pass at the root should always run to completion without a timeout check since it's cheap, guaranteeing a valid move exists as a safety net.

Now I'm building the win-line bitmasks for all rows, columns, and diagonals of length 5 on the 6x6 board, plus a fallback that just picks the first empty cell if the search fails entirely.

Writing bit-trick checks...

Writing rotation function code...

Now I'm sketching the search function: for each rotation direction and empty cell, I compute the resulting move bitboard, dedupe transposed states with a seen set, and check whether the move creates a five-in-a-row win for either side before recursing further.

If not terminal, at depth 1 it just evaluates the position statically, otherwise it queues the child for deeper recursive search with alpha-beta pruning and negamax scoring, sorting children by heuristic value first to improve pruning efficiency. Terminal wins get handled immediately so they short-circuit the rest of the loop.

I still need to define the full-board condition (only one empty cell left after the move), and figure out how to convert an internal cell index back into a human-readable move string with row, column, quadrant, and rotation direction. Then at the root level I want iterative deepening, increasing search depth incrementally until I hit a time limit, while tracking the best move found so far.

For root move ordering, I'll sort candidate moves by their values from the previous depth iteration and run full alpha-beta search on them at increasing depths, cutting the search early if a forced win is detected. I'll cap the total time budget around 0.75 seconds to leave a safety margin against overruns.

Checking timing at each node entry costs little overhead, and even at deeper nodes with many children the overshoot stays within a few milliseconds. I'm also verifying that the evaluation function correctly assigns values from the mover's perspective for the negamax framing, and confirming draws score zero properly.

I'm setting up threat weights based on piece counts in a line, adding center bonuses for quadrant centers, and thinking about whether depth-3 search is even feasible given the branching factor—probably too expensive without more pruning.

I also want to add exception handling so the policy always falls back to a legal move, and make sure input cells are safely cast to plain ints since they might be numpy types. Now I'm defining a popcount helper that uses the built-in bit_count when available, falling back to a bin-string count otherwise, and precomputing quadrant masks and starting offsets for the board evaluation.

Building rotation lookup table...

Defining line masks for streak detection...

Confirming the diagonal offset stays within bounds, then I move to writing an evaluation function that scores lines by counting weighted piece patterns for each side, adding bonuses where one side dominates a line the opponent hasn't touched.

Now I'm building the main policy function: converting the board grids into bitmask representations of my pieces and the opponent's, finding empty cells, setting a fallback move in case of timeout, and calling into the move-selection search.

For choose(), I'm generating root-level candidate moves across all 8 rotational symmetries, deduplicating by resulting position, checking for immediate wins, and scoring terminal states before sorting children by static evaluation to prioritize the search.

Now I'm iteratively deepening from depth 2 upward, running alpha-beta negamax search on each root candidate, tracking the best value found, and re-sorting roots after each depth so the strongest move is explored first next iteration -- with a timeout catch to bail out gracefully if the deadline hits mid-search.

I'm reasoning about whether partial results from a timed-out iteration should still be trusted: since roots are compared against alpha starting from the previous best move, any improvement discovered before timing out is likely genuine, so it's reasonable to accept a newly discovered better move even from an incomplete depth iteration.

Draw evaluations of 0 are fine since static evals can exceed that easily. I'm adding a deadline check that raises a timeout when the clock runs out, plus a shortcut for the single-empty-cell leaf case. I'll guard the five-in-a-row check so it only runs once a player has at least four pieces, keeping the depth-1 evaluation loop cheap.

Wins found deeper in the tree get valued less than shallower ones via WIN minus ply, and children are sorted by evaluated score from the mover's perspective before recursing. I'm also thinking about deduplicating children by rotation symmetry, since some quadrant configurations produce identical board states across rotations.

I double check the move string formatting and quadrant indexing scheme, confirm recursion depth is safe in Python, and verify the timing budget: precomputation is negligible and the initial root search across all moves takes only a few milliseconds, well within the time limit.

A transposition table could speed things up but adds risk of bugs, so I decide to skip it. Depth 3 completing mid-to-late game should be good enough, and when every move loses I just pick the max value anyway.

I verify the weight table for line evaluation and confirm that lines with pieces from both sides correctly contribute zero score, then move to writing the final implementation.
